claim: Broadly neutralizing antibodies (bnAbs) that neutralize diverse variants of a particular virus are of considerable therapeutic interest.
source: Broadly neutralizing antibodies (bnAbs) that neutralize diverse variants of a particular virus are of considerable therapeutic interest.
evidence: This is a statement about the therapeutic interest in bnAbs, supported by established scientific knowledge in the field.

claim: Eliciting broadly neutralizing antibodies through vaccination remains challenging, in part due to limited understanding of how antibodies evolve breadth.
source: Recent advances have enabled us to isolate and engineer these antibodies as therapeutics, but eliciting them through vaccination remains challenging, in part due to our limited understanding of how antibodies evolve breadth.
evidence: This claim is supported by inference from the current state of the field and the challenges described.

claim: CH65 is an anti-influenza receptor binding site (RBS) broadly neutralizing antibody.
source: Here, we analyze the landscape by which an anti-influenza receptor binding site (RBS) bnAb, CH65, evolved broad affinity to diverse H1 influenza strains.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the antibody being studied, supported by citation to prior work.

claim: An antibody library of all possible evolutionary intermediates between the unmutated common ancestor (UCA) and the affinity-matured CH65 antibody was generated.
source: We do this by generating an antibody library of all possible evolutionary intermediates between the unmutated common ancestor (UCA) and the affinity-matured CH65 antibody and measure the affinity of each intermediate to three distinct H1 antigens.
evidence: This describes the experimental approach taken in the study, supported by the data generated.

claim: Affinity to each antigen requires a specific set of mutations distributed across the variable light and heavy chains that interact non-additively (epistatically).
source: We find that affinity to each antigen requires a specific set of mutations – distributed across the variable light and heavy chains – that interact non-additively (i.e., epistatically).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Sets of mutations form a hierarchical pattern across antigens, with increasingly divergent antigens requiring additional epistatic mutations beyond those required to bind less divergent antigens.
source: These sets of mutations form a hierarchical pattern across the antigens, with increasingly divergent antigens requiring additional epistatic mutations beyond those required to bind less divergent antigens.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the data analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: Epistasis between heavy chain mutations and a mutation in the light chain at the VH-VL interface is essential for binding a divergent H1.
source: We investigate the underlying biochemical and structural basis for these hierarchical sets of epistatic mutations and find that epistasis between heavy chain mutations and a mutation in the light chain at the VH-VL interface is essential for binding a divergent H1.
evidence: This is a finding from structural and biochemical analyses presented in the manuscript.

claim: This is the first work to comprehensively characterize epistasis between heavy and light chain mutations.
source: Collectively, this is the first work to comprehensively characterize epistasis between heavy and light chain mutations and shows that such interactions are both strong and widespread.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the work, supported by the comprehensive nature of the data.

claim: Epistasis is a general feature of antibody sequence-affinity landscapes that can potentiate and constrain the evolution of breadth.
source: Together with our previous study analyzing a different class of anti-influenza antibodies, our results implicate epistasis as a general feature of antibody sequence-affinity landscapes that can potentiate and constrain the evolution of breadth.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the current study and previous work, supported by data and inference.

claim: The diversity of influenza poses an ongoing public health challenge as vaccination and natural infection typically elicit immune responses that are highly strain-specific.
source: The diversity of influenza poses an ongoing public health challenge as vaccination and natural infection typically elicit immune responses that are highly strain-specific, and hence quickly lose efficacy as the virus evolves (Kubo and Miyauchi, 2020; Angeletti and Yewdell, 2018; Neher and Bedford, 2015; Dugan et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature on influenza immunity.

claim: There has been substantial interest in vaccination strategies that elicit broadly neutralizing antibodies (bnAbs) that neutralize diverse strains of influenza.
source: This limited efficacy has garnered substantial interest in vaccination strategies that elicit broadly neutralizing antibodies (bnAbs) that neutralize diverse strains of influenza (Corti et al., 2017; Angeletti and Yewdell, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature on influenza bnAbs.

claim: Over the past two decades, there has been considerable effort to isolate and characterize anti-influenza bnAbs.
source: Over the past two decades, there has been considerable effort to isolate and characterize anti-influenza bnAbs (Whittle et al., 2011; Throsby et al., 2008; Corti et al., 2011; Dreyfus et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature on influenza bnAbs.

claim: Anti-influenza bnAbs target various conserved epitopes on the hemagglutinin (HA) influenza surface glycoprotein, including the receptor binding site (RBS), the stem or stalk domain, the lateral patch, and the membrane-proximal anchor site.
source: These bnAbs target various conserved epitopes on the hemagglutinin (HA) influenza surface glycoprotein, including the receptor binding site (RBS) (Whittle et al., 2011), the stem or stalk domain (Corti et al., 2011; Dreyfus et al., 2012; Ekiert et al., 2009), the lateral patch (Raymond et al., 2018), and the membrane-proximal anchor site (Guthmiller et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature on influenza bnAbs.

claim: BnAbs vary in germline gene usage and breadth, with some binding several strains within an HA subtype and others binding nearly all characterized influenza strains.
source: BnAbs also vary in germline gene usage and breadth, with some binding several strains within an HA subtype and others binding nearly all characterized influenza strains (Corti et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature on influenza bnAbs.

claim: We do not fully understand the evolutionary processes through which broadly neutralizing antibodies mature.
source: Despite the immense body of work on influenza bnAbs, we still do not fully understand the evolutionary processes through which they mature (Jiang et al., 2013; Horns et al., 2019; Sangesland and Lingwood, 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature and represents a knowledge gap in the field.

claim: Strategies to elicit broadly neutralizing antibodies remain limited.
source: Our strategies to elicit them therefore remain limited.
evidence: This is an inference from the limited understanding of bnAb evolution.

claim: Distinct antibodies with diverse sequences can target the same HA epitope and evolve broad reactivity.
source: It is clear, however, that distinct antibodies with diverse sequences can target the same HA epitope and evolve broad reactivity (Schmidt et al., 2013; Dreyfus et al., 2012; Ekiert et al., 2009; Schmidt et al., 2015a; Wu et al., 2020a).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature on influenza bnAbs.

claim: The redundancy of antibodies targeting the same epitope suggests that there are many possible evolutionary pathways to influenza bnAbs.
source: This redundancy suggests that there are many possible evolutionary pathways to influenza bnAbs.
evidence: This is an inference from the observation of diverse antibodies targeting the same epitope.

claim: The relatively low frequencies at which broadly neutralizing antibodies are observed in human repertoires following vaccination suggest that there are factors constraining their maturation that we do not yet fully appreciate.
source: Still, the relatively low frequencies at which they are observed in human repertoires following vaccination suggest that there are factors constraining their maturation that we do not yet fully appreciate (Wu et al., 2017; Bajic et al., 2019; Horns et al., 2020; Abbott et al., 2018; Andrews et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature and represents an inference about constraints on bnAb evolution.

claim: High-throughput mutagenesis approaches are widely used as a tool to understand key properties shaping the evolution of numerous proteins.
source: High-throughput mutagenesis approaches are widely used as a tool to understand key properties shaping the evolution of numerous proteins (Starr et al., 2017; Miton and Tokuriki, 2016; Bank et al., 2015; Phillips et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature on high-throughput mutagenesis.

claim: New mutations can differentially impact distinct protein functions and often interact non-additively (i.e., epistatically), potentially constraining the order in which they can occur.
source: This work has revealed that new mutations can differentially impact distinct protein functions and often interact non-additively (i.e., epistatically), potentially constraining the order in which they can occur (Weinreich et al., 2006; Gong et al., 2013; Sailer and Harms, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature on epistasis in protein evolution.

claim: High-throughput mutagenesis studies of antibodies have largely been limited to examining the effects of single mutations.
source: For antibodies, high-throughput mutagenesis studies have largely been limited to examining the effects of single mutations, either through saturating mutagenesis (e.g., deep mutational scanning) of relatively small regions (Wu et al., 2017; Adams et al., 2016; Forsyth et al., 2013) or through random mutagenesis (e.g., error-prone PCR) (Li et al., 2018; Amon et al., 2020; Bowers et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature on antibody mutagenesis studies.

claim: Saturating mutagenesis approaches can identify single amino acid substitutions that improve affinity to different subsets of strains but typically reduce breadth.
source: For example, this approach identified many single amino acid substitutions in the anti-influenza bnAb C05 that improve affinity to different subsets of strains but typically reduce breadth (Wu et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work on the C05 antibody.

claim: A key limitation of saturating mutagenesis approaches is that they cannot probe how epistatic interactions between mutations might constrain antibody evolutionary trajectories.
source: A key limitation of saturating mutagenesis approaches is that they cannot probe how epistatic interactions between mutations might constrain antibody evolutionary trajectories, which typically involve multiple mutations (Victora and Nussenzweig, 2012).
evidence: This is an inference about the limitations of saturating mutagenesis, supported by citation.

claim: Antibodies acquire numerous mutations and experience fluctuating selection pressures on short timescales.
source: Because antibodies acquire numerous mutations and experience fluctuating selection pressures on short timescales (Victora and Nussenzweig, 2012; Smith et al., 2004), they are necessarily distinct from other proteins for which epistasis has been studied.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature on antibody evolution.

claim: Antibodies bind antigens through disordered loops, in contrast to the structured active sites of most enzymes.
source: Moreover, they bind antigens through disordered loops, in contrast to the structured active sites of most enzymes, and they are relatively tolerant to mutations (Braden et al., 1998; Burks et al., 1997; Chen et al., 1999; Klein et al., 2013; Corti and Lanzavecchia, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature on antibody structure and function.

claim: The evolutionary dynamics of affinity maturation are defined by discrete rounds of mutation and selection compared to the more continuous processes most proteins are subject to.
source: Further, the evolutionary dynamics of affinity maturation are defined by discrete rounds of mutation and selection compared to the more continuous processes most proteins are subject to, and thus mutations that occur concurrently are selected based on their collective rather than individual effects (Victora and Nussenzweig, 2012; Unniraman and Schatz, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature on affinity maturation.

claim: The evolutionary constraints on antibodies may be unique.
source: For these reasons, the evolutionary constraints on antibodies may be unique.
evidence: This is an inference from the unique features of antibody evolution described.

claim: Epistasis is a key determinant of antibody affinity.
source: The few studies that have examined epistasis in antibodies indicate that it is a key determinant of affinity (Schmidt et al., 2013; Phillips et al., 2021; Pappas et al., 2014; Adams et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature on epistasis in antibodies.

claim: Multiple studies have identified mutations that interact synergistically to bind an antigen.
source: For example, multiple studies have identified mutations that interact synergistically to bind an antigen (Schmidt et al., 2013; Phillips et al., 2021; Pappas et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature on synergistic mutations in antibodies.

claim: Most work on epistasis in antibodies has focused on interactions between a small subset of mutations.
source: Still, most of this work has focused on interactions between a small subset of mutations (Schmidt et al., 2013; Xu et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature on epistasis in antibodies.

claim: Addressing the prevalence and general importance of epistasis in shaping antibody evolution will require more comprehensive combinatorial mutagenesis strategies.
source: Addressing the prevalence and general importance of epistasis in shaping antibody evolution will require more comprehensive combinatorial mutagenesis strategies that sample combinations of mutations present in each somatic antibody sequence (Phillips et al., 2021).
evidence: This is an inference about what is needed to understand epistasis in antibodies, supported by citation.

claim: In previous work, the relationship between antibody sequence and affinity (the sequence-affinity landscape) was systematically mapped across mutational landscapes relevant for the somatic evolution of two stem-targeting bnAbs of varying breadth, CR6261 and CR9114.
source: In previous work, we systematically mapped the relationship between antibody sequence and affinity (the sequence-affinity landscape) across mutational landscapes relevant for the somatic evolution of two stem-targeting bnAbs of varying breadth, CR6261 and CR9114 (Phillips et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a reference to prior work by the authors, supported by citation.

claim: Affinity was determined by nonadditive interactions between mutations, and such epistasis could both constrain and potentiate the acquisition of breadth.
source: We found that affinity was determined by nonadditive interactions between mutations, and that such epistasis could both constrain and potentiate the acquisition of breadth.
evidence: This is a finding from prior work by the authors, supported by citation.

claim: For CR6261, epistatic interactions were similar for binding distinct group 1 strains, thus evolutionary pathways could simultaneously improve in affinity to divergent antigens.
source: For CR6261, epistatic interactions were similar for binding distinct group 1 strains, thus evolutionary pathways could simultaneously improve in affinity to divergent antigens.
evidence: This is a finding from prior work by the authors, supported by citation.

claim: For CR9114, increasingly divergent antigens required additional epistatically interacting mutations such that evolutionary pathways were constrained to improve in affinity to one antigen at a time.
source: For CR9114, increasingly divergent antigens required additional epistatically interacting mutations such that evolutionary pathways were constrained to improve in affinity to one antigen at a time.
evidence: This is a finding from prior work by the authors, supported by citation.

claim: The distinct topologies of sequence-affinity landscapes result from differences between the various antigens and the mutations that are required for binding.
source: The distinct topologies of these sequence-affinity landscapes result from differences between the various antigens and the mutations that are required for binding.
evidence: This is an inference from prior work by the authors.

claim: Anti-stem bnAbs are among the broadest influenza bnAbs characterized.
source: Although anti-stem bnAbs are among the broadest influenza bnAbs characterized, they are a small and biased subset of the influenza antibody response.
evidence: This is supported by established knowledge in the field.

claim: The stem is minimally mutated amongst circulating viral strains and does not appear to be evolving in response to anti-stem antibodies.
source: Despite the presence of anti-stem antibodies in human sera (Yassine et al., 2018) and the ability to drive viral escape mutants in vitro (Wu et al., 2020b), the stem is minimally mutated amongst circulating viral strains and does not appear to be evolving in response to these antibodies, possibly due to the high concentration of antibody required for protection (Ellebedy, 2018; Han et al., 2021) and immune pressure.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature on anti-stem antibodies.

claim: RBS-directed bnAbs frequently make contacts with immunodominant epitopes surrounding the pocket that have substantial antigenic variation.
source: In contrast, due to the small size of the RBS pocket, RBS-directed bnAbs frequently make contacts with immunodominant epitopes surrounding the pocket that have substantial antigenic variation (Whittle et al., 2011; Schmidt et al., 2015b; Lee et al., 2014; Krause et al., 2011; Guthmiller et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature on RBS-directed bnAbs.

claim: RBS-directed bnAbs have a relatively narrower reactivity profile compared to anti-stem bnAbs.
source: Although RBS-directed bnAbs have a relatively narrower reactivity profile compared to anti-stem bnAbs, they are potently neutralizing, do not require effector functions for potent in vivo protection as do anti-stem bnAbs (Corti et al., 2011; DiLillo et al., 2014), and have evolved broad recognition despite the accumulation of antibody escape mutations in the periphery of the RBS.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature on RBS-directed bnAbs.

claim: RBS-directed bnAbs can mature from diverse germline VH and VL genes.
source: Further, RBS-directed bnAbs can mature from diverse germline VH and VL genes (Schmidt et al., 2015b), suggesting that there are likely numerous evolutionary pathways to target this epitope.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature on RBS-directed bnAbs.

claim: CH65 is a well-characterized RBS-directed bnAb that binds and neutralizes diverse H1 strains.
source: Specifically, we examine the influence of epistasis on the evolution of a well-characterized RBS-directed bnAb, CH65, which binds and neutralizes diverse H1 strains (Whittle et al., 2011; Schmidt et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature on CH65.

claim: CH65 was isolated from a donor 7 days post-vaccination.
source: CH65 was isolated from a donor 7 days post-vaccination.
evidence: This is a factual statement about the isolation of CH65.

claim: The unmutated common ancestor (UCA) and an early intermediate (I-2) of CH65 have moderate affinity for a subset of H1 strains that circulated early in the donor's lifetime.
source: The unmutated common ancestor (UCA) and an early intermediate (I-2) have moderate affinity for a subset of H1 strains that circulated early in the donor's lifetime (Whittle et al., 2011; Schmidt et al., 2015a).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature on CH65.

claim: The affinity-matured CH65 has 18 mutations throughout the light (VL) and heavy (VH) variable regions.
source: The affinity-matured CH65 has 18 mutations throughout the light (VL) and heavy (VH) variable regions, which improve affinity to strains that circulated early in the donor's life and confer affinity to antigenically drifted strains (Schmidt et al., 2013; Xu et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature on CH65.

claim: CH65 evolved to acquire affinity to emerging strains without compromising affinity for previously circulating strains.
source: Thus, CH65 evolved to acquire affinity to emerging strains without compromising affinity for previously circulating strains.
evidence: This is an inference from the affinity data for CH65.

claim: The structural changes upon affinity maturation of CH65 and clonally related antibodies have been extensively characterized.
source: The structural changes upon affinity maturation of CH65 and clonally related antibodies have been extensively characterized (Whittle et al., 2011; Schmidt et al., 2013; Schmidt et al., 2015a).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature on CH65.

claim: CH65 primarily matures by preconfiguring the HCDR3 loop into its binding conformation, thereby minimizing the conformational entropic cost of binding.
source: This work showed that CH65 primarily matures by preconfiguring the HCDR3 loop into its binding conformation, thereby minimizing the conformational entropic cost of binding (Schmidt et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature on CH65.

claim: None of the 18 somatic mutations in CH65 are in the HCDR3.
source: Importantly, none of the 18 somatic mutations are in the HCDR3; rather, key mutations in HCDR1, HCDR2, and LCDR1 result in contacts that stabilize the HCDR3 loop in its binding-compatible conformation (Schmidt et al., 2013; Xu et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature on CH65.

claim: Key mutations in HCDR1, HCDR2, and LCDR1 result in contacts that stabilize the HCDR3 loop in its binding-compatible conformation.
source: Importantly, none of the 18 somatic mutations are in the HCDR3; rather, key mutations in HCDR1, HCDR2, and LCDR1 result in contacts that stabilize the HCDR3 loop in its binding-compatible conformation (Schmidt et al., 2013; Xu et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature on CH65.

claim: Structural characterization and molecular dynamics simulations identified specific mutations that are critical for breadth, including some that interact synergistically to stabilize the HCDR3 loop.
source: This structural characterization, in addition to molecular dynamics simulations, identified specific mutations that are critical for breadth, including some that interact synergistically to stabilize the HCDR3 loop (Schmidt et al., 2013; Xu et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature on CH65.

claim: Many mutations in CH65 are important for imparting affinity to HA, including those at distant sites.
source: Given that many mutations in CH65 are important for imparting affinity to HA, including those at distant sites (Schmidt et al., 2013), we hypothesized that there are many sets of epistatic mutations in CH65 not previously identified, particularly because long-range epistatic interactions are difficult to predict from structural analyses alone.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature on CH65 and represents a hypothesis.

claim: CH65 engages HA through both light and heavy chain contacts and requires mutations in both chains to bind divergent antigens.
source: In contrast to the anti-stem bnAbs described above (Dreyfus et al., 2012; Lingwood et al., 2012), CH65 engages HA through both light and heavy chain contacts and requires mutations in both chains to bind divergent antigens (Schmidt et al., 2013; Xu et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature on CH65.

claim: Mutations in CH65 likely interact epistatically both within and between the heavy and light chains.
source: Thus, it is likely that mutations interact epistatically both within and between the heavy and light chains.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the structure and function of CH65.

claim: Characterizations of inter-chain epistasis have so far been limited to small sets of a few mutations.
source: Despite the potential importance of these interactions in shaping the evolution of CH65, and the numerous other antibodies that engage antigens using both chains (Corti et al., 2011; Schmidt et al., 2015a; Xiao et al., 2019; Ekiert and Wilson, 2012), characterizations of inter-chain epistasis have so far been limited to small sets of a few mutations (Schmidt et al., 2013; Xu et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature on inter-chain epistasis.

claim: A combinatorially complete antibody library containing all possible evolutionary intermediates between the UCA and the mature somatic sequence (N=216 = 65,536) was generated.
source: Here, to elucidate the role of epistasis (both inter- and intra-chain) in shaping the evolution of an RBS antibody, we systematically characterize the CH65 sequence-affinity landscape. Specifically, we generate a combinatorially complete antibody library containing all possible evolutionary intermediates between the UCA and the mature somatic sequence (N=216 = 65,536) and measure affinity to three antigenically distinct H1 strains to assess how epistasis can shape evolutionary pathways, leading to varying levels of breadth.
evidence: This describes the experimental approach taken in the study.

claim: Strong high-order epistasis constrains maturation pathways to bind antigenically distinct antigens.
source: We find that strong high-order epistasis constrains maturation pathways to bind antigenically distinct antigens.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the data analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: Fewer epistatic mutations are needed to bind an antigen similar to that bound by the UCA, and these sets of mutations overlap with those required to bind a more divergent antigen.
source: Although fewer epistatic mutations are needed to bind an antigen similar to that bound by the UCA, these sets of mutations overlap with those required to bind a more divergent antigen.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the data analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: These landscapes provide mechanistic insight into how affinity maturation responds to an evolving epitope and how exposure history can influence future immune responses.
source: Collectively, these landscapes provide mechanistic insight into how affinity maturation responds to an evolving epitope and how exposure history can influence future immune responses.
evidence: This is an inference from the data and analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: In combination with previous work on anti-stem bnAbs, this work shows how epistasis can differentially impact the evolutionary trajectories of bnAbs of varying breadth, epitope, and variable chain gene usage.
source: In combination with our previous work on anti-stem bnAbs (Phillips et al., 2021), this work shows how epistasis can differentially impact the evolutionary trajectories of bnAbs of varying breadth, epitope, and variable chain gene usage.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the current study and previous work.

claim: Q1E and S75A mutations in VH do not significantly impact binding affinity.
source: This library contains all possible combinations of mutations present in both the variable heavy and light chains of CH65, less two mutations (Q1E and S75A in VH) distant from the paratope that do not significantly impact binding affinity (Figure 1A, Figure 1—figure supplement 1) or physically interact with other residues.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Removing Q1E and S75A mutations results in a final library size of 216.
source: Removing these mutations results in a final library size of 216, which is within the throughput limit of our methods.
evidence: This is a factual statement about the library design.

claim: The UCA has weak affinity for MA90 but does not bind MA90-G189E or SI06.
source: Consistent with previous work (Schmidt et al., 2013; Xu et al., 2015), the UCA has weak affinity for MA90 but does not bind MA90-G189E or SI06; I-2 (which contains G31D, M34I, and N52H (VH)) has improved affinity to MA90, weak affinity to MA90-G189E, and does not bind SI06; and CH65 has near maximal affinity amongst library variants for all three antigens (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1B and citations to prior work.

claim: I-2 has improved affinity to MA90, weak affinity to MA90-G189E, and does not bind SI06.
source: Consistent with previous work (Schmidt et al., 2013; Xu et al., 2015), the UCA has weak affinity for MA90 but does not bind MA90-G189E or SI06; I-2 (which contains G31D, M34I, and N52H (VH)) has improved affinity to MA90, weak affinity to MA90-G189E, and does not bind SI06; and CH65 has near maximal affinity amongst library variants for all three antigens (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1B and citations to prior work.

claim: CH65 has near maximal affinity amongst library variants for all three antigens.
source: Consistent with previous work (Schmidt et al., 2013; Xu et al., 2015), the UCA has weak affinity for MA90 but does not bind MA90-G189E or SI06; I-2 (which contains G31D, M34I, and N52H (VH)) has improved affinity to MA90, weak affinity to MA90-G189E, and does not bind SI06; and CH65 has near maximal affinity amongst library variants for all three antigens (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The entire library binds MA90.
source: While the entire library binds MA90, ~83% of variants bind MA90-G189E and ~51% of variants bind SI06 (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: ~83% of variants bind MA90-G189E.
source: While the entire library binds MA90, ~83% of variants bind MA90-G189E and ~51% of variants bind SI06 (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: ~51% of variants bind SI06.
source: While the entire library binds MA90, ~83% of variants bind MA90-G189E and ~51% of variants bind SI06 (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: For all antigens, affinity is higher for more mutated variants, except for a subset of highly mutated variants that do not bind SI06.
source: For all antigens, affinity is higher for more mutated variants, except for a subset of highly mutated variants that do not bind SI06 (Figure 1B, bottom right).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: There are ~2000 variants that bind MA90 with reduced affinity relative to the UCA.
source: There are ~2000 variants that bind MA90 with reduced affinity relative to the UCA; none of these variants have detectable affinity for SI06, and only one has detectable affinity for MA90-G189E (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: All variants that bind SI06 also bind MA90-G189E.
source: Further, all variants that bind SI06 also bind MA90-G189E (Figure 1B) as variants can bind MA90-G189E with fewer mutations than SI06 (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1B and 1C.

claim: Variants can bind MA90-G189E with fewer mutations than SI06.
source: Further, all variants that bind SI06 also bind MA90-G189E (Figure 1B) as variants can bind MA90-G189E with fewer mutations than SI06 (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The hierarchical pattern observed in CH65, where mutations that enable binding to more antigenically divergent strains are dependent on mutations that enable binding to less divergent strains, is reminiscent of what was observed previously for the anti-stem bnAb CR9114.
source: This 'hierarchical' or 'nested' pattern, where mutations that enable binding to more antigenically divergent strains are dependent on mutations that enable binding to less divergent strains, is reminiscent of what we observed previously for the anti-stem bnAb CR9114 (Phillips et al., 2021), despite the comparatively subtle differences between the antigens examined here (83–96% epitope identity versus 52–61% for the CR9114 antigens) (Dreyfus et al., 2012; Schmidt et al., 2015a).
evidence: This is a comparison to prior work by the authors, supported by citations.

claim: Several mutations improve affinity to MA90 and MA90-G189E (e.g., Y35N, Y48C, D49Y (VL) and G31D, Y33H, H35N, N52H (VH)).
source: This analysis reveals that several mutations improve affinity to MA90 and MA90-G189E (e.g., Y35N, Y48C, D49Y (VL) and G31D, Y33H, H35N, N52H (VH)), and some of these distributions are multimodal, indicating that their effect on affinity depends on the presence of other mutations (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Some mutations improve affinity to MA90 and/or MA90-G189E on the UCA or I-2 backgrounds (e.g., Y35N (VL) and Y33H, H35N (VH)) and others on the CH65 background (Y48C, D49Y (VL)).
source: Consistent with this, some mutations improve affinity to MA90 and/or MA90-G189E on the UCA or I-2 backgrounds (e.g., Y35N (VL) and Y33H, H35N (VH)) and others on the CH65 background (Y48C, D49Y (VL)).
evidence: This is an inference from the data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: N52H dramatically improves affinity to SI06 and most variants lacking this mutation do not have detectable affinity.
source: For SI06, N52H dramatically improves affinity and most variants lacking this mutation do not have detectable affinity.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Several mutations (e.g., Y35N (VL)) improve affinity to SI06 in the I-2, but not the UCA, background.
source: Thus, several mutations (e.g., Y35N (VL)) improve affinity to SI06 in the I-2, but not the UCA, background (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The effects of mutations correlate between the different antigens, with mutations affecting affinity more substantially for MA90-G189E and SI06 compared to MA90.
source: In general, the effects of these mutations correlate between the different antigens, with mutations affecting affinity more substantially for MA90-G189E and SI06 compared to MA90 (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The mutations enriched amongst binders form a hierarchical pattern between the antigens.
source: Consistent with the landscapes in Figure 1B, we observe that the mutations enriched amongst binders form a hierarchical pattern between the antigens (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: A few mutations are enriched (≥55% frequency) amongst variants with nanomolar affinity for MA90 (e.g., Y35N, D49Y (VL) and Y33H, N52H (VH)).
source: For example, a few mutations are enriched (≥55% frequency) amongst variants with nanomolar affinity for MA90 (e.g., Y35N, D49Y (VL) and Y33H, N52H (VH)), a few additional mutations are enriched amongst MA90-G189E binders (e.g., S29R (VL) and G31D, H35N, R87K (VH)), and still additional mutations are enriched amongst SI06 binders (e.g., N26D, Y48C, V98I (VL) and M34I, R85G (VH)) (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2C and 2D.

claim: A few additional mutations are enriched amongst MA90-G189E binders (e.g., S29R (VL) and G31D, H35N, R87K (VH)).
source: For example, a few mutations are enriched (≥55% frequency) amongst variants with nanomolar affinity for MA90 (e.g., Y35N, D49Y (VL) and Y33H, N52H (VH)), a few additional mutations are enriched amongst MA90-G189E binders (e.g., S29R (VL) and G31D, H35N, R87K (VH)), and still additional mutations are enriched amongst SI06 binders (e.g., N26D, Y48C, V98I (VL) and M34I, R85G (VH)) (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2C and 2D.

claim: Still additional mutations are enriched amongst SI06 binders (e.g., N26D, Y48C, V98I (VL) and M34I, R85G (VH)).
source: For example, a few mutations are enriched (≥55% frequency) amongst variants with nanomolar affinity for MA90 (e.g., Y35N, D49Y (VL) and Y33H, N52H (VH)), a few additional mutations are enriched amongst MA90-G189E binders (e.g., S29R (VL) and G31D, H35N, R87K (VH)), and still additional mutations are enriched amongst SI06 binders (e.g., N26D, Y48C, V98I (VL) and M34I, R85G (VH)) (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2C and 2D.

claim: Y35N (VL) is depleted amongst SI06 binders.
source: Thus, except for Y35N (VL), which is interestingly depleted amongst SI06 binders (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), the mutations that enhance affinity to the three antigens form a hierarchical pattern.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The optimal order model for affinity is fourth-order for MA90 and fifth-order for MA90-G189E and SI06.
source: Using a cross-validation approach, we find that the optimal order model for affinity is fourth-order for MA90 and fifth-order for MA90-G189E and SI06, and we report coefficients at each order from these best-fitting models (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by the cross-validation analysis and data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: For all three antigens, there is widespread epistasis between mutations in the same chain and between mutations in different chains, with many epistatic terms exceeding first-order effects in magnitude.
source: For all three antigens, we find widespread epistasis between mutations in the same chain and between mutations in different chains, with many epistatic terms exceeding first-order effects in magnitude (Figure 3).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3.

claim: There are many strong epistatic interactions between mutations that are too distant to physically interact.
source: In contrast to our previous work on variable heavy-chain-only antibody landscapes (Phillips et al., 2021), we find many strong epistatic interactions between mutations that are too distant to physically interact (Figure 3—figure supplements 1–4).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplements 1–4.

claim: Mutations with strong first-order and epistatic effects often make contact with either HA or with the HCDR3 that engages the RBS.
source: When we examine the structural context of this epistasis, we find that mutations with strong first-order and epistatic effects often make contact with either HA or with the HCDR3 that engages the RBS (Figure 3B, Figure 3—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This is supported by structural analysis and data shown in Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 5.

claim: The effects of mutations with strong first-order and epistatic effects are either mediated through the contacts that they make with HA or through affecting the HCDR3 loop conformation.
source: This suggests that the effects of these mutations are either mediated through the contacts that they make with HA or through affecting the HCDR3 loop conformation.
evidence: This is an inference from the structural analysis.

claim: Mutations interact epistatically for each of the three antigens, though the magnitude of epistasis is higher for SI06 (explaining ~34% of the variance in KD, relative to ~24% for MA90, and ~25% for MA90-G189E).
source: These mutations interact epistatically for each of the three antigens, though the magnitude of epistasis is higher for SI06 (explaining ~34% of the variance in KD, relative to ~24% for MA90, and ~25% for MA90-G189E, see Figure 3—figure supplement 6).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 6.

claim: Epistatic interactions are essential for the acquisition of affinity to both MA90-G189E and SI06.
source: Importantly, these epistatic interactions are essential for the acquisition of affinity to both MA90-G189E and SI06.
evidence: This is supported by the data and structural analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: The I-2 intermediate (which contains G31D, M34I, N52H (VH)) is amongst the least-mutated variants that binds MA90-G189E.
source: The I-2 intermediate (which contains G31D, M34I, N52H (VH)) is amongst the least-mutated variants that binds MA90-G189E (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The N52H mutation would potentially clash with one of the binding-incompatible HCDR3 conformations observed in crystal structures of the UCA and I-2.
source: The N52H mutation, which substantially improves affinity to MA90-G189E (Figure 4A), would potentially clash with one of the binding-incompatible HCDR3 conformations observed in crystal structures of the UCA and I-2; thus, this mutation may increase the occupancy of the binding-compatible HCDR3 conformation (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by structural analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: N52H may increase the occupancy of the binding-compatible HCDR3 conformation.
source: The N52H mutation, which substantially improves affinity to MA90-G189E (Figure 4A), would potentially clash with one of the binding-incompatible HCDR3 conformations observed in crystal structures of the UCA and I-2; thus, this mutation may increase the occupancy of the binding-compatible HCDR3 conformation (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on structural analysis.

claim: In the bound state, N52H π-stacks with Y33H and hydrogen bonds with G31D.
source: In the bound state, N52H π-stacks with Y33H and hydrogen bonds with G31D (Figure 4B and C, Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by structural analysis shown in Figure 4B, 4C, and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: N52H and G31D form a network of interactions between HCDR1, HCDR2, and the 150-loop of HA to stabilize the binding interaction.
source: Consequently, N52H and G31D, which together provide high affinity for MA90-G189E (Figure 4A), form a network of interactions between HCDR1, HCDR2, and the 150-loop of HA to stabilize the binding interaction (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by structural analysis shown in Figure 4C.

claim: G31D and M34I (I-2) reduce the dissociation rate by ~3.5–5-fold to improve affinity.
source: Thus, while N52H alone confers affinity to MA90-G189E, G31D and M34I (I-2) reduce the dissociation rate by ~3.5–5-fold to improve affinity (Figure 4C, Figure 4—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This is supported by kinetics data shown in Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 5.

claim: The interactions between N52H, G31D, and M34I are distant (~15–20 Å) from the residue conferring viral escape, precluding any direct interaction.
source: Notably, these interactions are distant (~15–20 Å) from the residue conferring viral escape, precluding any direct interaction (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by structural analysis shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The I-2 mutations (G31D, M34I, N52H) are insufficient to confer appreciable affinity to SI06 in the absence of other epistatic mutations.
source: Though these mutations are also important for affinity to the antigenically drifted SI06, they are insufficient to confer appreciable affinity in the absence of other epistatic mutations (Figure 4D, top).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Y35N in the light chain and H35N in the heavy chain interact synergistically with the I-2 mutations (G31D, M34I, N52H) to confer affinity to SI06.
source: In examining the minimally mutated variants that can bind SI06, we find that Y35N in the light chain and H35N in the heavy chain interact synergistically with the I-2 mutations (G31D, M34I, N52H) to confer affinity to SI06 (Figure 4D, bottom).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The hierarchical sets of mutations that confer broad reactivity to these antigens do so through epistasis.
source: Thus, the hierarchical sets of mutations that confer broad reactivity to these antigens (Figure 2D) do so through epistasis.
evidence: This is an inference from the data presented.

claim: The germline residue Y35 in the light chain framework (FWR) 2 is part of a cluster of aromatic residues at the VH-VL interface and makes π-stacking, methionine–aromatic, and hydrogen bonding interactions between LFWR2 and LCDR3, HCDR3, and HFWR4.
source: In particular, the germline residue Y35 in the light chain framework (FWR) 2 is part of a cluster of aromatic residues at the VH-VL interface and makes π-stacking, methionine–aromatic, and hydrogen bonding interactions between LFWR2 and LCDR3, HCDR3, and HFWR4 (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is supported by structural analysis shown in Figure 4E.

claim: The somatic mutation Y35N effectively removes interactions with the HCDR3.
source: The somatic mutation Y35N effectively removes these interactions with the HCDR3.
evidence: This is supported by structural analysis.

claim: The observed changes in affinity from Y35N are attributed to the loss of hydrogen bonding between LFWR2 and HCDR3.
source: Although the loss of the aromatic moiety from tyrosine to asparagine likely has a destabilizing effect, we attribute the observed changes in affinity to the loss of hydrogen bonding between LFWR2 and HCDR3; this is in part because the lineage member CH67, which has similarly broad reactivity, acquires a Y35F mutation upon affinity maturation that is only a removal of a hydroxyl group, preventing the ability to form hydrogen bonding interactions through the side chain (Schmidt et al., 2013).
evidence: This is an inference supported by structural analysis and comparison to CH67.

claim: H35N removes a methionine–aromatic interaction between the HFWR2 and HCDR3.
source: Similarly, H35N removes a methionine–aromatic interaction, known to have a stabilizing effect in proteins (Valley et al., 2012), between the HFWR2 and HCDR3 (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is supported by structural analysis shown in Figure 4E and citation to prior work.

claim: Addition of Y35N and H35N into the UCA background did not confer affinity to SI06.
source: Addition of Y35N and H35N into the UCA background did not confer affinity to SI06 (Figure 4D and E).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4D and 4E.

claim: The addition of H35N into the I-2 background produced weak but detectable affinity with an association rate that was improved upon addition of Y35N.
source: However, the addition of H35N into the I-2 background produced weak but detectable affinity with an association rate that was improved upon addition of Y35N (Figure 4D and E, Figure 4—figure supplement 6).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4D, 4E, and Figure 4—figure supplement 6.

claim: While Y35N confers affinity to SI06 for variants with few somatic mutations, the magnitude of this effect diminishes as the number of mutations increases.
source: Notably, while Y35N confers affinity to SI06 for variants with few somatic mutations, the magnitude of this effect diminishes as the number of mutations increases.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Y35N is depleted amongst the highest affinity variants.
source: Indeed, Y35N is depleted amongst the highest affinity variants (Figure 2C, Figure 2—figure supplement 1) and in the context of a mutated background decreased the association rate and overall affinity (Figure 4E), suggesting that Y35N, which removes inter-chain contacts, is likely only beneficial during early rounds of affinity maturation.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2C, Figure 2—figure supplement 1, and Figure 4E.

claim: Y35N, which removes inter-chain contacts, is likely only beneficial during early rounds of affinity maturation.
source: Indeed, Y35N is depleted amongst the highest affinity variants (Figure 2C, Figure 2—figure supplement 1) and in the context of a mutated background decreased the association rate and overall affinity (Figure 4E), suggesting that Y35N, which removes inter-chain contacts, is likely only beneficial during early rounds of affinity maturation.
evidence: This is an inference from the data.

claim: Previous studies on the CH65 lineage showed that HCDR3 rigidification contributed to high-affinity binding to SI06.
source: Previous studies on this lineage (Schmidt et al., 2013; Xu et al., 2015) showed that HCDR3 rigidification contributed to high-affinity binding to SI06: crystal structures of the unbound, affinity-matured Fabs had the same HCDR3 configurations as those in the antigen-bound state; the UCA and I-2, however, were either disordered or constrained, due to crystal packing, in a binding-incompatible state.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The mutations Y35N and H35N were insufficient to rigidify the HCDR3 as observed by the HCDR3 conformation and high B factors or the lack of density corresponding to the HCDR3.
source: These variants were insufficient to rigidify the HCDR3 as observed by the HCDR3 conformation and high B factors or the lack of density corresponding to the HCDR3 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by structural data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The I-2 mutations conferred affinity towards MA90-G189E by stabilizing the HCDR1 and HCDR2 with HA and were required for the addition of Y35N and H35N, which remove contacts with HCDR3, to confer affinity against SI06 without complete HCDR3 rigidification.
source: These data show that the I-2 mutations conferred affinity towards MA90-G189E by stabilizing the HCDR1 and HCDR2 with HA and were required for the addition of Y35N and H35N, which remove contacts with HCDR3, to confer affinity against SI06 without complete HCDR3 rigidification, revealing a biophysical mechanism through which inter-chain epistasis can determine broad affinity in a hierarchical manner.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the structural and kinetics data.

claim: Mutational trajectories leading to CH65 are most favorable in sequential selection scenarios that begin with MA90 and end with SI06, consistent with the donor's likely exposure history.
source: This pathway likelihood inference reveals that mutational trajectories leading to CH65 are most favorable in sequential selection scenarios that begin with MA90 and end with SI06, consistent with the donor's likely exposure history (Schmidt et al., 2013; Schmidt et al., 2015a).
evidence: This is supported by the pathway analysis and citations to prior work.

claim: The MA90-SI06 sequential scenarios are considerably more likely than either antigen alone, a mixture of antigens, or SI06-MA90 sequential scenarios.
source: Further, the MA90-SI06 sequential scenarios are considerably more likely than either antigen alone, a mixture of antigens, or SI06-MA90 sequential scenarios.
evidence: This is supported by the pathway analysis shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Mutations on the UCA background can improve affinity to MA90 but not to SI06, so MA90 is favored as the selecting antigen initially.
source: Mutations on the UCA background can improve affinity to MA90 but not to SI06, so MA90 is favored as the selecting antigen initially.
evidence: This is an inference from the pathway analysis.

claim: After a few mutations, MA90 reaches maximal affinity and cannot improve further, at which point mutations begin to improve SI06 affinity.
source: After a few mutations, however, MA90 reaches maximal affinity and cannot improve further, at which point mutations begin to improve SI06 affinity.
evidence: This is an inference from the pathway analysis.

claim: Selection with MA90 favors mutations that enable the acquisition of SI06 affinity and would be unlikely to occur under selection with SI06 alone.
source: These constraints reflect the structure of the sequence-affinity landscape: selection with MA90 favors mutations that enable the acquisition of SI06 affinity and would be unlikely to occur under selection with SI06 alone.
evidence: This is an inference from the pathway analysis.

claim: Scenarios that begin with MA90 or MA90-G189E and end with SI06 are most likely when considering all three antigens.
source: Similarly, when we consider all three antigens, we find that scenarios that begin with MA90 or MA90-G189E and end with SI06 are most likely, again reflecting the hierarchical nature of the sequence-affinity landscape (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by the pathway analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Two of the I-2 mutations (G31D and N52H) and the epistatic mutations that interact with the HCDR3 (e.g., Y33H, H35N, and Y35N) are most likely to occur early in mutational trajectories, especially in scenarios that begin with MA90 selection.
source: Even when we do not constrain pathways to pass through I-2, we find that two of the I-2 mutations (G31D and N52H) and the epistatic mutations that interact with the HCDR3 (e.g., Y33H, H35N, and the previously uncharacterized Y35N) are most likely to occur early in mutational trajectories, especially in scenarios that begin with MA90 selection.
evidence: This is supported by the pathway analysis shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The highly synergistic HCDR3-stabilizing mutations Y48C and D49Y are most likely to occur late, and consecutively, with D49Y preceding the otherwise-deleterious Y48C.
source: Additionally, the highly synergistic HCDR3-stabilizing mutations Y48C and D49Y are most likely to occur late, and consecutively, with D49Y preceding the otherwise-deleterious Y48C.
evidence: This is supported by the pathway analysis shown in Figure 5C.

claim: When pathways are constrained to pass through I-2, Y35N is the most probable subsequent mutation, and this likelihood rapidly decreases with additional mutations.
source: Consistent with our structural analyses, we find that when pathways are constrained to pass through I-2, Y35N is the most probable subsequent mutation, and this likelihood rapidly decreases with additional mutations.
evidence: This is supported by the pathway analysis shown in Figure 5C.

claim: When considering all possible pathways in the optimal antigen selection scenario, I-2 is not the most likely 3-mutation intermediate, suggesting that the evolution of CH65 was not contingent on passing through I-2.
source: However, when we consider all possible pathways in the optimal antigen selection scenario, I-2 is not the most likely 3-mutation intermediate, suggesting that the evolution of CH65 was not contingent on passing through I-2 (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by the pathway analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: The likelihood of passing through the I-2 intermediate is ~55% higher than that expected by chance.
source: Still, the likelihood of passing through the I-2 intermediate is ~55% higher than that expected by chance – it is a minimally mutated antibody with improved affinity to MA90 and MA90-G189E, and it contains the N52H mutation that is essential for SI06 affinity.
evidence: This is supported by the pathway analysis.

claim: While there are many accessible paths to CH65, the three mutations in I-2 result in rapid improvements in affinity and breadth and favor subsequent selection for epistatic mutations that ultimately provide the breadth of CH65.
source: Thus, while there are many accessible paths to CH65, the three mutations in I-2 result in rapid improvements in affinity and breadth and favor subsequent selection for epistatic mutations that ultimately provide the breadth of CH65.
evidence: This is an inference from the pathway analysis.

claim: The breadth of an RBS influenza bnAb, CH65, is determined by high-order epistatic interactions that differ between divergent antigens.
source: Collectively, we find that the breadth of an RBS influenza bnAb, CH65, is determined by high-order epistatic interactions that differ between divergent antigens (Figure 5—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is a summary of the findings from the study.

claim: Epistasis in CH65 is widespread within and between both the heavy and light chains.
source: This epistasis is widespread within and between both the heavy and light chains.
evidence: This is a summary of the findings from the study.

claim: This is the first comprehensive study of inter-chain epistasis.
source: To our knowledge, this is the first comprehensive study of inter-chain epistasis and illustrates the extent to which mutations can differentially impact affinity depending on the presence of other mutations, even those too far apart to physically interact.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the work.

claim: The maturation of antibodies that engage antigen with both chains may be distinct compared to those that do not.
source: This suggests that the maturation of antibodies that engage antigen with both chains may be distinct compared to those that do not.
evidence: This is an inference from the findings.

claim: There are more opportunities for epistatic interactions across two chains compared to just one, and the degree of both intra- and inter-chain epistasis is likely contingent on the chain pairing.
source: There are more opportunities for epistatic interactions across two chains compared to just one, and the degree of both intra- and inter-chain epistasis is likely contingent on the chain pairing.
evidence: This is an inference from the findings.

claim: Understanding the nature of inter-chain epistasis may be useful for designing therapeutic antibodies and eliciting broadly protective immune responses.
source: Given the importance of both light and heavy chain mutations across diverse bnAbs (Corti et al., 2011; Schmidt et al., 2015a; Xiao et al., 2019; Ekiert and Wilson, 2012), understanding the nature of this epistasis may be useful for designing therapeutic antibodies and eliciting broadly protective immune responses.
evidence: This is an inference about the implications of the findings.

claim: The epistasis that confers broad reactivity in CH65 is mediated through sets of mutations that both interact with HA and those that do not interact with HA.
source: Further, our structural analysis shows that the epistasis that confers broad reactivity in this antibody is mediated through sets of mutations that both interact with HA and those that do not interact with HA.
evidence: This is a summary of the structural analysis findings.

claim: Epistatic mutations add or remove interactions between CDRs, FWRs, and chains that act by different mechanisms of stabilizing the binding conformation (e.g., G31D and N52H) or removing constraints on the HCDR3 (e.g., Y35N and H35N).
source: These epistatic mutations add or remove interactions between CDRs, FWRs, and chains that act by different mechanisms of stabilizing the binding conformation (e.g., G31D and N52H) or removing constraints on the HCDR3 (e.g., Y35N and H35N).
evidence: This is a summary of the structural analysis findings.

claim: The Y35N mutation effectively removes interactions between the LFWR2 and the HCDR3 at the VH-VL interface and mediates affinity improvement to a more antigenically advanced influenza strain by increasing the association rate.
source: The Y35N mutation effectively removes interactions between the LFWR2 and the HCDR3 at the VH-VL interface and mediates affinity improvement to a more antigenically advanced influenza strain by increasing the association rate.
evidence: This is a summary of the structural and kinetics analysis findings.

claim: An analogous observation was noted for the anti-HIV bnAb CH103 that co-evolved during a natural infection within a single individual.
source: An analogous observation was noted for the anti-HIV bnAb CH103 that co-evolved during a natural infection within in a single individual (Liao et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Structural studies of CH103 identified mutations at the VH-VL interface that were associated with reconfiguration of the HCDR3 to enable broad reactivity against a viral escape variant.
source: Structural studies of CH103 identified mutations at the VH-VL interface (which is the region containing residue 35 in CH65) that were associated with reconfiguration of the HCDR3 to enable broad reactivity against a viral escape variant (Fera et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Antibodies can evolve to bind viral escape variants by modulating the VH-VL interface and the HCDR3 configuration, in response to both chronic (HIV) and punctuated (influenza) exposures.
source: Although additional work will be needed to address the generality of this finding, it appears that antibodies can evolve to bind viral escape variants by modulating the VH-VL interface and the HCDR3 configuration, in response to both chronic (HIV) and punctuated (influenza) exposures.
evidence: This is an inference from the findings and comparison to prior work.

claim: Y35N may function to initially increase flexibility, enabling acquisition of affinity to SI06 after acquiring mutations in the heavy chain, and subsequent maturation rigidified the HCDR3.
source: Consequently, Y35N may function to initially increase flexibility, enabling acquisition of affinity to SI06 after acquiring mutations in the heavy chain, and subsequent maturation rigidified the HCDR3.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the data.

claim: This increased flexibility followed by rigidification is reminiscent of molecular dynamics studies of anti-HIV bnAbs that suggest initial increases in flexibility may provide a means to sample additional conformational space prior to rigidification.
source: This increased flexibility followed by rigidification is reminiscent of molecular dynamics studies of anti-HIV bnAbs that suggest initial increases in flexibility may provide a means to sample additional conformational space prior to rigidification (Ovchinnikov et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Increasingly divergent antigens require additional epistatically interacting mutations, resulting in a hierarchical pattern of mutations that improve affinity to distinct antigens.
source: In comparing CH65 mutations that improve affinity to diverse H1 antigens, we find that increasingly divergent antigens require additional epistatically interacting mutations, resulting in a hierarchical pattern of mutations that improve affinity to distinct antigens.
evidence: This is a summary of the findings.

claim: The I-2 mutations (e.g., G31D, M34I, N52H) may compensate for the G189E mutation by stabilizing interactions with HA opposite this site, potentially allowing the antibody to shift to relieve the clash.
source: The I-2 mutations (e.g., G31D, M34I, N52H) may compensate for the G189E mutation by stabilizing interactions with HA opposite this site, potentially allowing the antibody to shift to relieve the clash; a similar observation was made for another RBS-directed antibody (McCarthy et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the structural analysis and comparison to prior work.

claim: The I-2 mutations help to stabilize binding in the antigenically distant SI06 but do not sufficiently compensate for the loss of potential contacts between the HCDR3 and the RBS (e.g., ∆K133a and E156G) within the antigen combining site; further mutations Y35N and H35N that likely influence HCDR3 conformations are needed.
source: These same mutations help to stabilize binding in the antigenically distant SI06 but do not sufficiently compensate for the loss of potential contacts between the HCDR3 and the RBS (e.g., ∆K133a and E156G) within the antigen combining site; further mutations Y35N and H35N that likely influence HCDR3 conformations are needed.
evidence: This is an inference from the structural and kinetics analysis.

claim: Mutations confer broad reactivity in the CH65 lineage in a hierarchical manner.
source: These structural observations and the data generated here suggest that mutations confer broad reactivity in the CH65 lineage in a hierarchical manner.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the data and structural analysis.

claim: The hierarchical landscape of CH65 is not as striking as that of CR9114, where larger sets of mutations are required to bind substantially more divergent antigens.
source: Although the hierarchical landscape of CH65 is not as striking as that of CR9114 (Phillips et al., 2021), where larger sets of mutations are required to bind substantially more divergent antigens, it is intriguing that the landscape for a considerably narrower bnAb can also have this structure.
evidence: This is a comparison to prior work by the authors.

claim: Hierarchical sequence-affinity landscapes may be quite common, as they are not unique to CR9114, to anti-stem bnAbs, or to bnAbs that engage distinct HA subtypes.
source: This suggests that hierarchical sequence-affinity landscapes may be quite common, as they are not unique to CR9114, to anti-stem bnAbs, or to bnAbs that engage distinct HA subtypes.
evidence: This is an inference from the findings.

claim: If hierarchical sequence-affinity landscapes are common amongst bnAbs, they may contribute to the low frequencies of bnAbs in human repertoires.
source: If hierarchical sequence-affinity landscapes are common amongst bnAbs, they may contribute to the low frequencies of bnAbs in human repertoires.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the findings.

claim: For bnAbs with hierarchical landscapes, epistatically interacting mutations are required to bind a given antigen, additional epistatic mutations (that interact favorably with those acquired previously) are required to bind a distinct antigen, and so on.
source: For bnAbs with such landscapes, epistatically interacting mutations are required to bind a given antigen, additional epistatic mutations (that interact favorably with those acquired previously) are required to bind a distinct antigen, and so on.
evidence: This is a summary of the findings.

claim: The landscapes measured focus exclusively on mutations present in the affinity-matured antibodies, which are biased by the selection pressures those bnAbs experienced.
source: Importantly, the landscapes measured here and in our previous work focus exclusively on mutations present in the affinity-matured antibodies, which are biased by the selection pressures those bnAbs experienced.
evidence: This is a limitation of the study.

claim: While these landscapes show that diverse bnAbs can mature by acquiring hierarchical sets of epistatic mutations that are favored in sequential exposure regimens, there may be alternative mutational pathways to breadth that are not hierarchical and are favored in other exposure regimes.
source: Thus, while these landscapes show that diverse bnAbs can mature by acquiring hierarchical sets of epistatic mutations that are favored in sequential exposure regimens, there may be alternative mutational pathways to breadth that are not hierarchical and are favored in other exposure regimes.
evidence: This is a speculation about alternative pathways.

claim: The observation that antibodies can evolve breadth through hierarchical mutational landscapes lends support for vaccination with sequential doses of distinct antigens.
source: Still, the observation that antibodies can evolve breadth through hierarchical mutational landscapes lends support for vaccination with sequential doses of distinct antigens.
evidence: This is an inference about the implications of the findings.

claim: These findings are consistent with a recent study that demonstrates memory B cell recruitment to secondary germinal centers upon vaccination in humans, allowing for additional rounds of antibody maturation to antigenically drifted strains.
source: These findings are consistent with a recent study that demonstrates memory B cell recruitment to secondary germinal centers upon vaccination in humans, allowing for additional rounds of antibody maturation to antigenically drifted strains (Turner et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Sequential exposures with antigenically drifted strains may help elicit within-subtype potent bnAbs like CH65, in addition to the cross-subtype bnAbs described in previous work.
source: Here, we find that sequential exposures with antigenically drifted strains may help elicit within-subtype potent bnAbs like CH65, in addition to the cross-subtype bnAbs described in our previous work.
evidence: This is an inference from the findings.

claim: Several theoretical and computational models of bnAb affinity maturation favor sequential immunization strategies as they allow antibodies to acquire the mutations necessary to bind one antigen before experiencing selection pressure to bind another, ultimately producing bnAbs that have 'focused' on conserved epitopes.
source: Several theoretical and computational models of bnAb affinity maturation also favor sequential immunization strategies as they allow antibodies to acquire the mutations necessary to bind one antigen before experiencing selection pressure to bind another, ultimately producing bnAbs that have 'focused' on conserved epitopes (Wang et al., 2015; Sachdeva et al., 2020; Wang, 2017; Molari et al., 2020; Sprenger et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: This focusing process may occur by favoring selection on hierarchical sets of epistatically interacting mutations.
source: Our work indicates that this focusing process may occur by favoring selection on hierarchical sets of epistatically interacting mutations.
